content: The bond-analytics family (ACCRINTM, DISC, DURATION, MDURATION, INTRATE, PRICE, PRICEDISC, PRICEMAT, RECEIVED, YIELD, YIELDDISC, YIELDMAT) and the variable-declining-balance VDB are implemented by Excel, Google Sheets, the `formulas` Python library, and Lattice, but are absent from HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel, all three of which return #NAME? (unrecognized name). LibreOffice recorded blank for every case in this suite (see the separate LibreOffice harness-gap annotation). Among the four implementing engines the results agree: the closed-form functions (DISC, DURATION, MDURATION, PRICE, PRICEDISC, PRICEMAT, RECEIVED, INTRATE, ACCRINTM, VDB) match to roughly 1e-13 relative (last-ULP floating-point noise), while the yield functions (YIELD, YIELDDISC, YIELDMAT) are Newton/bisection root-finders and agree only to about 1e-9 because each engine uses its own tolerance and initial guess. Confirmed live: HyperFormula returns #NAME? for ACCRINT, PRICE, YIELD, VDB, and DISC.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (HyperFormula #NAME? for ACCRINT/PRICE/YIELD/VDB/DISC; DV-0001 documents the pycel gap)

content: ACCRINT diverges on the actual accrued-interest day count. For accrint-annual-basis-1 (=ACCRINT(DATE(2011,2,15), DATE(2011,8,15), DATE(2012,2,15), 0.0575, 1000, 1, 1), basis 1 = actual/actual) Excel and Google Sheets return 57.5, i.e. exactly one full annual coupon (1000*0.0575), treating issue-to-settlement as a whole period, whereas the `formulas` library returns 57.4208024552736 and Lattice returns 57.421340629274965 — both compute an actual-day fraction slightly below 1.0 and disagree with each other in the third digit. For accrint-semiannual (=ACCRINT(DATE(2008,3,1), DATE(2008,8,31), DATE(2011,2,15), 0.1, 1000, 2, 0), basis 0 = 30/360) three distinct answers appear: Excel 295.8333333333333, Google Sheets and Lattice 295.5555555555555, and `formulas` 295.2777777777778 — the engines apply the 30/360 handling of the 31st-of-month issue date and the first-coupon accrual counting differently. HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel return #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank. Confirmed live: `formulas` reproduces 57.4208024552736 and 295.2777777777778.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (formulas reproduces both values); needs Excel/gsheets confirmation of the 30/360 semiannual value

content: The Treasury-bill functions (TBILLEQ, TBILLPRICE, TBILLYIELD) are implemented by Excel, the `formulas` library, Google Sheets, HyperFormula, and Lattice, which agree to floating-point noise (e.g. TBILLEQ short-maturity 0.06697909461767572 vs HyperFormula's 0.066979094618). IronCalc computes the same functions but its recorded value is captured at reduced display precision, so it forms its own agreement class (0.067 for that case, 0.0942 for tbilleq-standard, 98.39 for tbillprice, 0.0616 and 0.0914 for tbillyield). This IronCalc reduced-precision read-back reproduces live and is not a stale fixture. pycel returns #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (IronCalc TBILLYIELD returns 0.0616 live, matching the fixture's reduced precision)

content: DOLLARDE is implemented by every engine except pycel, which returns #NAME?. The implementing engines (Excel, `formulas`, Google Sheets, HyperFormula, IronCalc, Lattice) all evaluate =DOLLARDE(1.16, 32) to 1.5, but split into two agreement classes purely from a one-ULP floating-point difference: 1.4999999999999998 versus 1.5. LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (1-ULP split; pycel #NAME? per DV-0001)

content: For these closed-form time-value functions Excel, the `formulas` library, Google Sheets, HyperFormula, and Lattice compute at full double precision and agree modulo last-digit floating-point noise. IronCalc computes the same underlying value but its recorded (and live) result is captured at reduced display precision, so it forms a distinct agreement class: e.g. CUMIPMT first-year -4966.49 (vs HyperFormula's -4966.4941306 and the full -4966.494130578189), PMT -995.51, NPER 360, DDB 26.84, NPV 124.76, DB 186083.33, MIRR 0.18 and 0.13, CUMPRINC -1475.37, IRR-growing 0.16. Confirmed live: IronCalc returns exactly these reduced-precision values, so it is a value-capture (format-rendering) property of the IronCalc driver, not a stale fixture or an algorithmic difference. pycel returns #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: live probe reproduced IronCalc's reduced-precision read-back for CUMIPMT/PMT/NPER/DDB/NPV/IRR/MIRR

content: These functions are iterative root-finders (Newton / bisection). The implementing engines all converge but stop at slightly different roots, so their last several digits disagree without any engine being wrong. RATE mortgage-implied spreads across 0.004166644536345589 (Excel), 0.004166644536359948 (formulas), 0.004166644536337786 (gsheets), and Lattice 0.00416664453636018 — differences near 1e-11. RATE zero-payment spreads similarly around 0.0717734625. IRR simple-project sits at a near-zero root, so residuals range from an exact 0 (gsheets) through 1.28e-17, 7.83e-18, 2.93e-17, up to Excel's 1.95e-12 — the engines simply halt at different tiny residuals. IronCalc reports reduced-precision values (0.071773463, 0.0041666445363, 0.16); pycel returns #NAME?; LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (spread pattern characteristic of iterative solvers; IronCalc reduced-precision confirmed live)

content: XIRR is a root-finder over irregular date-spaced cash flows. Excel converges to a slightly different root than the other implementing engines: xirr-simple-project gives Excel 0.3733625352382659 versus 0.37336253350955556 (formulas), 0.3733625335188316 (gsheets), and Lattice 0.3733625335095561 — a ~1e-8 solver-tolerance gap where Excel stands alone. IronCalc reports the reduced-precision 0.373362534. HyperFormula and pycel do not implement XIRR and return #NAME? (confirmed live: HyperFormula returns #NAME? for XIRR with both serial and text date seeds). LibreOffice recorded blank. Note the date column was seeded as ISO text, which every XIRR-implementing engine here coerces (unlike XNPV — see the XNPV annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (HyperFormula XIRR #NAME?); Excel-alone root is solver tolerance

content: XNPV splits on how each engine handles a dates argument supplied as text. In the corpus the date column was seeded as ISO strings (e.g. "2020-01-01"). Excel, Google Sheets, and HyperFormula reject text dates and return #VALUE!, whereas the `formulas` library, IronCalc, and Lattice coerce the ISO strings to date serials and compute a number (908.8535548268738 for xnpv-single-future-flow, 2086.647602031535 for xnpv-standard). This was confirmed live and isolated to the seed type: HyperFormula's XNPV returns a number (908.85355483) when the same dates are seeded as numeric serials but #VALUE! when they are seeded as strings; IronCalc and `formulas` return the number for both seed types. The practical portability rule: XNPV date cells must hold real dates (numeric serials), not text, or the strict engines error. pycel returns #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: live probe (HyperFormula XNPV: number on serial dates, #VALUE! on string dates; IronCalc/formulas coerce both)

content: For =IPMT(0.05/12, 360, 360, -200000) — the interest portion of the final payment of a 360-period loan — Excel, Google Sheets, HyperFormula, IronCalc, and Lattice all compute the small positive residual interest (~4.4549512283), agreeing to floating-point noise. The `formulas` Python library instead returns #NUM! for this last-period case (confirmed live). pycel returns #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: live probe (formulas returns #NUM!; the five other implementing engines return ~4.4550)

content: =RRI(0, 1000, 2000) has an invalid period count of zero, so the return-rate computation involves a 1/nper exponent that is undefined. Excel, the `formulas` library, HyperFormula, IronCalc, and Lattice all surface this as #NUM! (confirmed live for HyperFormula, IronCalc, and `formulas`), while Google Sheets surfaces the same invalid input as #DIV/0! — an error-code difference over the identical failing computation. pycel returns #NAME? (function absent); LibreOffice recorded blank.

_meta.evidence: live probe (HyperFormula/IronCalc/formulas all #NUM!); fixture shows gsheets alone at #DIV/0!

content: In these cases the implementing engines do not substantively diverge — they agree exactly (PV zero-rate 1000; RATE unreachable #NUM! for all) or only at last-ULP floating-point noise (CUMPRINC full-life ~-100000, ISPMT mid-loan ~-64814.8148, PPMT first-period ~240.3099). The fork exists only because pycel returns #NAME? (function absent, per DV-0001) and LibreOffice recorded blank. IronCalc, where present, sits inside the main agreement class.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (computing engines agree exactly or to ULP; only pycel/libreoffice split the class)

content: =NPV(0, 100, 200, 300) evaluates to 600 in every engine that ran it, including pycel — the only outlier is LibreOffice, which recorded blank. Because LibreOffice recorded blank for the entire financial corpus while LibreOffice Calc is well known to implement NPV (and all these functions), this blank is almost certainly a harness/recording gap rather than genuine engine behavior, and the case should be re-recorded before treating the fork as real.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (all engines incl pycel = 600; libreoffice blank across the whole suite points to a harness gap)
